clue.text: Sounds like the path leading to the altar

indicators.note: the clue says the word for the path is only heard, its spelling being a different word

parts.note: a bridle path, or bridleway, is a track for horses; the path here is the bridle

explanation.surface: Someone describes the aisle a bride walks up to the altar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like' tells you that BRIDLE (as in bridle path) is pronounced the same as the answer, which is spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything to do with a bride or a wedding, such as the walk up the aisle, is described by this adjective.

clue.text: In 1965 the subject of an unlimited audit

definitions.text: In 1965 the subject of an unlimited audit

parts.words: In 1965 the subject of an unlimited audit
parts.note: an audit with its first and last letters lost leaves UDI, the Unilateral Declaration of Independence made by the white minority government of an African colony in 1965

explanation.surface: An accountant recalls a big inspection of the books back in 1965.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the first and last letters from 'audit' and you get UDI, the Unilateral Declaration of Independence. In 1965 Ian Smith's government declared independence from Britain for this southern African colony.
explanation.definitionFit: The African colony now called Zimbabwe declared independence from Britain unilaterally in November 1965.

clue.text: One who translates female attire ultimately into male

parts.note: drag is women's clothing worn by a man

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the next word, into

parts.note: a man is a male

explanation.surface: A translator describes a man who ends up wearing women's clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes only the last letter of 'into', an O, to sit between DRAG and MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragoman was an interpreter and guide in Turkish, Arabic or Persian-speaking countries.

clue.text: Delayed recovery of side

parts.note: something delayed is late
a rally is a recovery, as in prices or health

explanation.surface: A slow recovery is reported from one flank.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateral means relating to the flank, so the adverb describes something done towards or concerning the flank.

clue.text: Hair spring inside to go wrong

indicators.note: inside tells you one piece sits within the letters of the other piece

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair
a spa is a mineral spring

explanation.surface: A hair spring tucked inside a watch is about to malfunction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts SPA within TRESS, after its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespass in the old biblical sense means to sin or commit an offence, to do wrong.

clue.text: Supplier of travellers' checks

parts.note: not a bank issuing traveller's cheques, but the railway official who checks passengers' tickets

explanation.surface: A bank or bureau that issues travellers' cheques.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests traveller's cheques; the checks are inspections of travellers' tickets on a train or at a station barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: This railway employee examines passengers' tickets, so supplies checks to those travelling.

clue.text: Staff exciting respect

indicators.note: exciting means stirring up, so the letters of the next word are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A member of staff behaves in a way that earns admiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exciting' rearranges RESPECT.
explanation.definitionFit: A staff is a rod carried as a symbol of office, and a monarch's ceremonial rod is exactly that.

clue.text: HMS Stone, of Yangtse fame

parts.note: a Royal Navy frigate trapped on the Yangtze River in 1949, named after a purple gemstone

explanation.surface: A warship famous for an episode on the Yangtze river.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1949 Yangtze Incident a British frigate was shelled and trapped by Chinese Communist forces before escaping downriver; the ship bore the name of a purple quartz.
explanation.definitionFit: The violet variety of quartz gave its name to the frigate in the 1949 Yangtze Incident.

clue.text: Was partial to liquor — but bandsman could carry it

parts.note: to have sided with someone is to have been partial to or supported them
rum is a liquor

explanation.surface: A bandsman who favoured spirits might carry a bottle on parade.
explanation.definitionFit: A small two-headed snare drum is slung at a marching musician's flank.

clue.text: But such a novelist has a classical spasm

parts.note: classical refers to ancient Greece and Rome, so Roman fits
a tic is a twitch or spasm

explanation.surface: A writer of love stories is afflicted with a twitch of an old-fashioned sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such a novelist' is read as an adjective: the novelist is of the kind who writes love stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A novelist who writes love stories is described by the adjective for love and passion.

clue.text: Seen to suffer imprisonment

definitions.meaning: past tense of behold, to see or observe
split in two, the words say to ..., kept in custody

explanation.surface: A prisoner is observed being locked up.
explanation.definitionFit: The past form of behold means observed; split as two words it means detained in custody.

clue.text: A note to the head would .be expedient

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
the head of a river is its source

explanation.surface: Someone advises sending a memo to the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' means the head of a river, where it rises.
explanation.definitionFit: An expedient is a means of coping, the same as a way out or stand-by.

clue.text: Felt uneasy with the CID looking curious

indicators.note: looking curious means appearing odd, so the letters are made into a strange new order

explanation.surface: Someone is unsettled while detectives eye them inquisitively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looking curious' rearranges THE and CID; CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British plain-clothes police.
explanation.definitionFit: To have felt an irritating restless urge, as in itching to go, is to have felt uneasy.

clue.text: From a cell to a different place

indicators.note: different means changed, so the letters of these words are put in a changed order

explanation.surface: A prisoner is moved from their cell to somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges A CELL TO A; 'place' as a verb is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To assign or apportion something to a spot or person is to put it in position.

clue.text: A high level of ballet perhaps also

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters given are just one possible order, to be rearranged

parts.note: and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: A ballet reaches a lofty standard, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BALLET into TABLEL, followed by AND.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is high flat ground, a raised area of level land.

clue.text: Let uncle have a piece

definitions.meaning: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker, so letting him have something is pledging it for a loan

explanation.surface: Someone lets a relative have a share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is old British slang for a pawnbroker.
explanation.definitionFit: Pledging goods to a pawnbroker is one sense; the other is the lowliest chessman.

clue.text: Hitch-hiker's request for a drink

definitions.meaning: a hitch-hiker asks drivers for a lift
a restorative tonic or stiff drink

explanation.surface: A hitch-hiker asks a driver for something to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A thumber asks motorists to collect them; the phrase is also a restorative tonic or stiff drink.

clue.text: Argumentative mathematician

parts.note: a word meaning a person who argues noisily is also the title for a Cambridge student gaining first-class honours in mathematics

explanation.surface: A mathematician who loves a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: At Cambridge a student achieving first-class honours in the mathematics tripos is given this title; the ordinary word means one who disputes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a disputer, and at Cambridge it is the title for a first-class mathematics graduate.

clue.text: Skier's tempo-reducer, to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means only partly, so the answer is a run of letters partly found in the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Something a skier uses to slow down, partly described.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'extent' as the definition, but the answer does not mean extent: 'to some extent' is the hidden-word signal and the whole clue defines a stem turn, which slows a skier.
explanation.definitionFit: A stem turn, pushing the ski tails apart, is how a skier slows, so it reduces the skier's speed.

clue.text: The ocean's lower regions, home of the whelk and such

definitions.text: home of the whelk and such

parts.note: the ocean's waters are the seas
hell is the underworld, the lower regions

explanation.surface: The deepest parts of the ocean are where whelks and the like live.
explanation.definitionFit: A whelk lives inside a spiral marine casing, which is its house.

clue.text: Fade out Miss St Clare — change scene

parts.note: Little Eva St Clare is the child in Uncle Tom's Cabin

indicators.note: change tells you the letters of the next word are reordered

explanation.surface: A stage direction: Miss St Clare's scene fades out and the scene changes.
explanation.walkthrough: Eva St Clare is a character in Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel; 'change' rearranges SCENE into NESCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish gradually like vapour is to fade away.

clue.text: The least you can say

parts.note: not a minimal remark but the smallest unit of speech, as in not uttering a single one

explanation.surface: A remark about saying the minimum.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like 'the least you could say'; read literally it is the smallest unit you can utter.
explanation.definitionFit: A single unit of pronunciation is the smallest piece of a spoken word.

clue.text: Gag you won't hear

definitions.meaning: to gag someone is to stop them speaking, or the cloth used to do it
absence of sound, which you cannot hear

explanation.surface: A joke that goes unheard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a joke, but here it means muzzling someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Gagging someone means making them quiet; the noun also names the absence of any sound.

clue.text: Linked somehow to light

indicators.note: somehow suggests things done in some unknown way, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Two things are connected in some way to illumination.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue dropped 'Linked'; the page prints it. 'somehow' rearranges LINKED.
explanation.definitionFit: To set a fire going is to ignite it.

clue.text: Uniform with an air in one of the services

parts.note: uniform means even, regular
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A soldier in uniform sings a tune in one of the armed services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'services' are church services, not the armed forces the uniform suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening prayer in the Anglican church is a service of worship.

clue.text: Doctor's job 'ere in London

indicators.note: 'ere for here shows the speaker dropping the letter h, so the h is lost from the word

parts.note: a doctor's work is curing the sick

explanation.surface: A Cockney talks about a doctor's work around here in London.
explanation.walkthrough: ''ere' is 'here' with its H dropped, telling you to drop the H from HEALING. The answer is a district of west London, famous for its film studios.
explanation.definitionFit: A borough of west London, famous for its film studios and comedies.

clue.text: Turn from painting back to poetry

indicators.note: back says the word for painting is to be read in the opposite direction

parts.note: painting is an art
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: An artist switches from painting back to writing poems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ART into TRA, which is followed by VERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To swivel a gun sideways is to train it round, so the verb means to turn.

clue.text: Victualler quietly beheaded building inspector.

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly

indicators.note: beheaded tells you to cut off the first letter of the word

parts.note: a surveyor inspects buildings

explanation.surface: A supplier of food quietly decapitates a building inspector.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' removes the S from SURVEYOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A victualler supplies food and provisions, the same as a supplier or caterer.

clue.text: Melodious sound of stupid order to dog

indicators.note: sound of says the words are pronounced, giving a word spelt differently

parts.note: dull means slow-witted, stupid; sit is a command given to a dog

explanation.surface: A soothing voice gives a dim dog its instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound of' says DULL SIT, said quickly, is pronounced the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet, pleasant voice or tone is soothing to the ear.
